idiom_name: Data.define cases + case/in with a raising else
implementation_notes: Ruby 3.2's `Data.define(:number)` creates frozen, value-equal value objects with `deconstruct`/`deconstruct_keys`, and `case/in` (3.0+) matches them structurally - that pair is Ruby's stand-in for case classes, with the union expressed as a module of constants and every `case` expression ending in `else raise` because no `in` list is checked for completeness. Sealing does not exist: constants can be reopened, new classes can always be defined, and the closure is a naming/co-location convention. Static enforcement, if the project wants it, comes from an external checker - Sorbet's `T::Enum`, `sealed!` and `T.absurd` provide exactly the closed set plus exhaustiveness check at the cost of a gem, type annotations and a separate checking step. The classic abstract-base-plus-visitor design is not idiomatic Ruby; prefer `Data` plus one raising match funnel, or plain polymorphism when cases carry behaviour.
code_sketch:
module Payment
  Card     = Data.define(:number)
  Transfer = Data.define(:iban)
end

def describe(payment)
  case payment
  in Payment::Card(number)   then number
  in Payment::Transfer(iban) then iban
  else raise ArgumentError, "unknown payment #{payment.class}"
  end
end
pitfalls: `Data` freezes the object, not its contents: a member holding an Array or Hash stays mutable, so deep immutability needs frozen members or copies.
Without `else raise`, a `case/in` expression returns nil for an unrecognized variant - a silent nil that surfaces far from the match, and `in` clauses are order-sensitive.
Structural patterns do not check the class unless it is named: `in [number]` matches any deconstructable object, not only the intended case.
Constants are open and `Data` classes can be reopened or subclassed, so the closure is convention (Sorbet's `sealed!` is the closest static check and is not stdlib).
